response: The authors detail a systematic review methodology for assembling, filtering, and categorising literature corpora. They identify three corpora—Main (81.2 % of 1,263 publications), Implications (9.9 %), and Further (8.9 %)—and describe an automated acquisition pipeline, filtering strategies, and post‑processing steps for each set, aiming for coverage, transparency, volume management, and reproducibility. Figure 4 visualises the corpora and their publication proportions.

Robotic foundation models (RFMs) show promise for flexible, instruction‑driven robot control, yet their industrial applicability remains under‑investigated. This survey maps the RFM landscape, derives eleven industrial implications, and builds an assessment framework of 149 criteria covering model capabilities and ecosystem needs. Applying the framework to 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs via 48,276 LLM‑assisted, expert‑validated decisions reveals limited, uneven industrial maturity: even top models meet only a subset of criteria and display narrow, implication‑specific strengths rather than broad coverage. Progress toward industry‑grade RFMs requires systematic integration of safety, real‑time feasibility, robust perception, interaction, and cost‑effective, auditable system deployment.

The authors built a principal RFM‑related literature corpus to cover all major research directions on robotic foundation models (RFMs) and adjacent topics such as training protocols, extensions, applications, safety, robustness and adversarial challenges. They defined RFMs for control & integrated RFMs (Section 2) and excluded LLM‑based, high‑level or overly specialised approaches, labeling those “High‑Level”. Two large‑scale retrievals were run with an identical Python pipeline (Section 3.1) on 4 July 2025 (10 728 valid entries, 5 035 unique) and 30 Oct 2025 (12 027 valid entries, 4 999 unique). After merging and a cautious duplicate‑removal protocol, 6 497 unique articles formed the base corpus. A coarse LLM filter removed non‑robotics papers, retaining 4 834; a stricter LLM filter for RFM relevance yielded 1 408 articles, for which manual sampling found no false negatives. Manual review, enrichment and further de‑duplication produced the final main corpus of 1 025 unique, highly relevant works. These were categorised as: 341 control or integrated RFMs (324 on manipulation/mobile manipulation/general robotics, 17 on drones, surgical robots, locomotion, navigation or underwater), 321 related works (training protocols, extensions), 231 High‑Level articles (LLM‑based multi‑agent systems or narrowly scoped models), 77 data/benchmark papers, and 55 surveys/reviews (24 general embodied AI, 31 including RFMs, 11 focused on RFMs, only 2 on industrial relevance). This corpus underpins all subsequent review analyses, ensuring systematic coverage of RFMs and closely associated fields.

The introduction outlines a shift in industrial robotics from tightly‑engineered, isolated automation toward flexible, collaborative deployment, driven by the growing use of collaborative robots (cobots) that can be commissioned quickly, redeployed across changing processes, and operate near humans. Although cobots provide high mechanical precision, low power consumption, and repeatability, their industrial utility is increasingly constrained by the availability of robust, adaptive, and intuitive control methods rather than by actuation performance. This motivates a focus on learning‑based robot intelligence that can handle variability in tasks, environments, actuation, and sensing while meeting industrial constraints such as safety, reliability, low‑latency operation, and cost‑effective integration.

Recent advances in large‑scale learning have produced Foundation Models (FMs), which aim to reduce manual engineering by transferring knowledge across tasks. Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) extend this idea to embodied decision‑making, supplying a flexible platform for transfer across tasks, interfaces, and embodiments. The survey concentrates on RFMs that generate low‑level actions for direct robot actuation because this interface is central to real‑world deployment and tightly coupled to industrial constraints (latency, safety gating, hardware‑specific action spaces). Various model‑building paradigms are mentioned—diffusion‑based, dreaming‑based, and dual‑system designs—but architectural taxonomy is omitted in favor of an industrial lens that connects methodological progress to practical deployment constraints.

A hierarchical categorisation of robotic control methods is presented (Figure 1): (1) predefined/rule‑based (fixed trajectories, no dynamic adaptation); (2) reactive/parametrised (sensor‑driven limited adaptation); (3) specialised/narrow (task‑specific solutions); (4) foundational (broadly pretrained, efficiently fine‑tuned); and (5) generalist (zero‑/few‑shot, online adaptation with high‑level instructions). The hierarchy illustrates a trajectory from rigid, task‑specific automation toward adaptable, instruction‑driven operation with decreasing commissioning effort. The introduction of FMs marks the transition from specialised control (level 3) to foundational robotics (level 4), yet achieving true generalist systems (level 5) requires robust online adaptation, dependable instruction following, and safe operation under uncertainty—capabilities critical in dynamic, cost‑driven industrial settings.

Publication trends (Figure 2) show a sharp increase in RFMs‑related work, especially in 2025, raising concerns about fragmentation and inflated claims without structured industrial evaluation. Existing surveys lack a systematic, implication‑grounded assessment of industrial deployment readiness, prompting this review. The paper’s structure links foundational concepts to industrial requirements and then to a systematic assessment of current RFMs (Figure 3). After defining RFMs and positioning them within the control landscape (Section 2), the authors describe their review methodology and corpus composition (Section 3), discuss related works (Section 4), and provide background on cobot adoption and hardware constraints (Sections 5‑6).

The authors distil industrial deployment viewpoints into eleven interdependent implications (Section 7.1) and operationalise them into a criteria catalogue of 149 items for assessing industrial maturity (Section 7.3). They apply this framework to manipulation‑capable RFMs, presenting an overview and a criteria‑based maturity evaluation (Section 8), and conclude with a synthesis of findings (Section 9). A key preview is that, despite impressive benchmark progress and broader contributions, industrial maturity remains limited and uneven: current models typically address only a few enabling dimensions rather than providing integrated coverage of the deployment‑critical requirements prevalent in real industrial settings. This motivates the primary goal of moving discussion from isolated benchmark successes toward a traceable, implication‑grounded view of what constitutes a credible industrial RFM.

The authors motivate Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) as an extension of foundation models (FMs) that have proven effective in domains such as natural‑language processing, where large‑scale, heterogeneous pre‑training yields emergent capabilities far beyond the original objectives. They argue that robotics introduces distinct challenges: closed‑loop, high‑dimensional decision making in which actions continuously reshape the environment, and extreme heterogeneity of robot embodiments, configurations, and operational contexts. Classical control solutions are deterministic but narrowly tailored, lacking the task‑agnostic, cross‑embodiment generalisability required for industrial use. Consequently, the authors contend that foundational methods capable of leveraging diverse robotic datasets are needed to provide the same kind of emergent, adaptable performance seen in language models.

Definitions are clarified. Hu et al. distinguish “single‑purpose” RFMs (focused on a single modular capability such as perception, planning, or control) from “general‑purpose” RFMs that span perception, planning, control, and even non‑robotic tasks. The authors argue that only the latter, which integrate perception with actionable outputs (e.g., control, trajectory, or plan generation), qualify as true RFMs; models limited to perception or control alone are merely encoders, decoders, or specialised solutions. They also address terminology: while some works conflate Vision‑Language‑Action models (VLAs) with RFMs, the authors treat VLAs as a distinct sub‑category of RFMs. VLAs employ multimodal inputs—language and vision—to enable human‑like instructability and generate robot actions, aligning them with the RFM criteria of multimodality, output flexibility, and adaptability. Zhou et al. note that VLAs align all modalities into a common token format for end‑to‑end training; Xu et al. describe a typical VLA architecture of perception, reasoning/planning, and action modules, though the authors allow models without strict modular separation to count as VLAs. Zhong et al. emphasize that VLAs must bridge digital AI with embodied interaction, demanding robustness to real‑world complexity and hardware constraints.

Synthesising these perspectives, the authors define RFMs as highly adaptable, data‑driven models specialised for robotic tasks, distinguished by a “generalist core” that enables efficient adaptation across tasks, settings, embodiments, and hardware with minimal engineering or retraining (e.g., via high‑level instructions or flexible action representations). To satisfy this core, RFMs must exhibit: (1) Multi‑Modality – ingestion of diverse proprioceptive and exteroceptive signals such as sensor data, images, and natural language; (2) Output Flexibility – generation of actions, plans, trajectories, or similar outputs suitable for a spectrum of robots and domains; and (3) Adaptability – ability to generalise or adapt to new tasks, environments, or embodiments with little manual intervention.

Based on this definition, the authors categorise RFMs. VLAs are a prominent sub‑category because they meet the multimodal input and flexible output criteria, allowing intuitive prompting and low‑level actuation. Beyond VLAs, RFMs can be grouped by principal function: (a) RFMs for Control, which directly produce low‑level motor commands, joint velocities, or force/torque signals across diverse embodiments; (b) RFMs for Planning, which focus on high‑level reasoning, task decomposition, (re)planning, or explainability, often outputting sequential plans or sub‑goals for downstream controllers; and (c) Integrated RFMs, which jointly combine planning and control, aligning with the vision of general‑purpose robotic intelligence capable of internal reasoning, failure explanation, recovery, and long‑horizon planning with direct control. The authors note that planners align more closely with the overarching RFM paradigm because their outputs are predominantly high‑level.

The taxonomy also acknowledges models that lack natural‑language inputs yet still qualify as RFMs if they retain multimodal foundations and adaptability—for example, Vision‑Action models such as DP or Dreamitate, which use goal images or state representations. Specialized subclasses target particular domains (manipulation, locomotion/navigation, aerial, underwater, mobile‑manipulation) and often arise from predefined action spaces or fine‑tuning data. Manipulation is highlighted as especially pertinent for industrial deployment, underpinning tasks like assembly, pick‑and‑place, and dexterous handling, and is viewed as a central challenge whose solutions can support broader capabilities such as locomotion.

In summary, within this survey a model is considered an RFM only if it demonstrates a generalist core enabling cross‑task or cross‑embodiment adaptability, integrates multimodal inputs, and generates flexible outputs. Models lacking these properties are treated as specialised or narrow approaches rather than true RFMs.

The authors created a modular Python pipeline to automate literature acquisition while preserving reproducibility and breadth. Users supply one or more structured Academic Search Query Syntax (ASQS) queries, a publication‑date range (e.g., 2020‑present), chosen databases (arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus, Semantic Scholar), a retrieval preference (latest vs. most relevant), and per‑query upper limits (e.g., 100 results). The pipeline translates each ASQS query into the native syntax of each selected database, relaxes unsupported features, and executes all DB‑query permutations automatically. Returned metadata are merged, duplicates removed using identifiers such as DOIs, and missing metadata are fetched from auxiliary APIs (Semantic Scholar, arXiv, Crossref). Metadata validity is programmatically checked (e.g., title‑abstract consistency); articles lacking essential information or containing errors are excluded, followed by a second duplicate‑removal pass. Validated articles are stored as JSON/YAML (optionally PDF) with detailed fields and accompanied by auto‑generated reports describing queries, databases, time spans, result counts, timestamps, and per‑DB‑query statistics. An on‑demand GPT‑4o‑based filter scores semantic relevance, delivering binary labels, scores in [0, 1], and brief rationales; sequential filtering can apply stricter criteria. A separate GPT‑4o‑driven Query Proposal component generates initial query suggestions from the ASQS definition and user intent. Manual refinement is required only for the highlighted refinement steps; all other processes run automatically. After automated retrieval, the authors performed manual post‑processing (enrichment, correction, additional filters) to ensure quality, completeness, and relevance of the final corpora.

Industrial robotics is shifting from highly optimized, isolated automation toward flexible, collaborative cobots, creating a demand for robust, adaptive, and intuitive control methods rather than raw actuation performance. This survey defines robotic foundation models (RFMs) that generate low‑level actions, categorises control approaches from rule‑based to generalist systems, and presents an industrial‑grounded assessment framework comprising eleven viewpoints and 149 criteria to evaluate RFM maturity. Applying this framework to manipulation‑capable RFMs reveals impressive benchmark progress but limited, uneven industrial readiness, as current models typically address only a few deployment‑critical dimensions.

The authors expanded their review beyond the two primary corpora by conducting additional automated and manual searches covering industrial robots, cobots, compute hardware, sensors, manipulators, efficiency considerations, related fields, and norms/standards, which yielded 113 auxiliary publications that were incorporated into the development and writing of the work.

The authors built an industrial implication corpus to capture requirements, challenges, and context‑specific attributes of real‑world robotic applications. Using the modular literature pipeline from Section 3.1, they issued seven broad ASQS queries (Table B3) covering applications, case studies, analyses, and reviews, limited to publications from 2015 to July 2025 across arXiv, GoogleScholar, OpenAlex, Scopus, and SemanticScholar, retrieving up to 50 results per query (max 1,750). The search returned 1,240 valid entries, of which 892 were unique after deduplication. A coarse LLM‑based relevance filter (same intent as the original search) reduced the set to 296 relevant and 596 unrelated articles. The authors then manually reviewed the 125 most relevant articles (LLM relevance ≥ 0.9), deeming lower‑scored entries (< 0.9) outside the detailed review. Insights from this core set were iteratively synthesized, clustered, and mapped to industrial implications for robotic systems, with further discussion in Section 7.

The authors define Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) as highly adaptable, data‑driven systems that possess a generalist core enabling cross‑task and cross‑embodiment adaptability with minimal engineering or retraining, ingest multimodal proprioceptive, exteroceptive, and natural‑language inputs, and output flexible actions, plans or trajectories for diverse robots; they distinguish “single‑purpose” models (e.g., perception‑only or control‑only) from true RFMs, argue that Vision‑Language‑Action models (VLAs) are a prominent RFM sub‑category because they combine multimodal inputs and low‑level action generation, and further categorize RFMs into control‑focused, planning‑focused, and integrated models while noting that other multimodal approaches (e.g., vision‑action without language) also qualify if they exhibit the same generalist adaptability.

The authors expanded their literature base beyond the two primary corpora by conducting both automated and manual searches covering industrial robots, collaborative robots, compute hardware, sensors, manipulators, efficiency considerations, related fields, and relevant norms and standards. This effort yielded 113 auxiliary publications, which the authors state were incorporated into the development and writing of the present work. No additional methodological details, limitations, or evaluative comments are reported for this supplementary search.

source_label: Section: 5 Rise of Cobots in Industry
response: Recent advances in RFMs are mainly demonstrated alongside cobots, but these developments are frequently confined to laboratory, table‑top, or kitchen settings. To underscore the broader industrial relevance of this trend, the authors note the need to first consider the evolution of industrial robotics and the transition toward more collaborative robotic systems.

source_label: Section: 5.1 Landscape of Industrial Robotics: Tradition & Transformation
response: Industrial robots are defined as automatically controlled, reprogrammable multipurpose manipulators with three or more axes, requiring additional tooling (e.g., grippers, welding torches) and built on incomplete‑machine architectures. Their flexibility derives from complex kinematic chains with multiple rotational degrees of freedom, enabling mobility across many production processes. Traditional robots are programmed for predefined functions, need specialised expertise for reprogramming, operate at high speeds with large payloads, and are usually isolated from humans for safety, serving heavy‑duty, repetitive or hazardous tasks. Configurations include parallel (Delta), Cartesian, cylindrical, SCARA, spherical, and articulated serial types, ordered by increasing similarity to cobots. These conventional types lack flexibility, adaptability, safe direct human‑robot collaboration (HRC) and intuitive human‑robot interaction (HRI) demanded by modern manufacturing, especially SMEs. Cobots emerged to address these limits: initially passive devices for guided movement, they have evolved into articulated robots with lower payloads, reduced speeds, rounded geometries and sensor suites for real‑time contact or human detection, enabling safe intentional HRC. Cobots are designed for flexible deployment, intuitive HRI, rapid reconfiguration, minimal downtime and cost, supporting high product variability and small batch sizes. Their functional ethos differs from traditional robots: rather than replacing humans in isolated environments, cobots aim to augment human capability through joint execution of complex, variable, or ergonomically challenging tasks, prioritising safety, ease of integration and shared‑workflow efficiency.

The authors conducted an extensive literature review (Section 3.2) and identified 55 relevant survey and review articles, comprising a “survey corpus” whose composition is shown in Figure 9. The corpus includes works on general embodied AI (GEA), surveys that include robot foundation models (+RFMs), and those with an explicit industrial focus (IND). Of the 55 surveys, 11 (20 %) specifically target the robot foundation model (RFM) field; these are summarized in Table 1. All 11 focus on vision‑language agents (VLAs), a sub‑category of RFMs, and none present an explicit industrial focus. Only two of the RFM‑focused surveys diverge from a VLA‑centric approach: Zhou et al. [15] examine language‑conditioned manipulation, and Hu et al. [12] provide an overview of the broader RFM paradigm and current methodologies. The authors note that, despite many recent VL‑focused surveys, comprehensive investigation of the broader RFM concept remains largely unaddressed, with virtually no attention to other RFM sub‑categories such as Vision‑Action models or control‑oriented integrated RFMs (Section 2).

Regarding industrial relevance, Figure 9 and Table 2 show that only 2 of the 55 surveys (3.6 %) have a clear industrial application focus. Neither of these emphasizes the implications of RFMs for industry. Fan et al. [35] concentrates on vision‑language models (VLMs) for human‑robot collaboration in smart manufacturing, covering only a narrow subset of what the authors consider important for industrial robotics. Ren et al. [36] discuss general embodied intelligence and evaluate capabilities and limitations in industrial contexts, but do not consider specific models or the impact of industrial use cases on model design.

Synthesizing these findings, the authors highlight a pronounced gap: no existing survey is dedicated to the industrial application of RFMs or to how industrial use cases affect RFMs, even within the narrower VLA context. Existing industrial‑focused surveys are either overly general or limited to specific facets (e.g., VLMs in HRC). In contrast, the present work diverges from the prevailing emphasis on VLA architectures and functions; it provides a taxonomy, an extensive overview of the RFM landscape, and a detailed analysis of the attributes and capabilities demanded of RFMs by industrial use cases, outlining how such requirements should inform future RFM design and how industrial maturity can be evaluated.

Modern cobots, noted for greater flexibility and safety than traditional robots, have moved beyond labs into diverse real‑world sectors. In manufacturing and assembly they handle precision‑adaptable tasks such as assembly, pick‑and‑place, machine tending, quality inspection, palletising, packaging, material handling, welding and gluing; examples include UR10e units at PSA and Fiat Chrysler for door, hood and soft‑top assembly, riveting and mounting, plus pick‑and‑place in plant nurseries and packaging in board factories. For quality control they use advanced sensors and vision to inspect dimensions, assembly integrity and defects, e.g., UR3s checking automotive touchscreen panels. Integrated with AMRs, cobot arms enable mobile manipulation for intra‑factory logistics, moving components with MiR200 in appliance production and handling heavy or ergonomically difficult transports. In healthcare they assist patient handling, rehabilitation, medication dispensing, surgical assistance, tool manipulation and remote ultrasound/endoscope positioning. Agricultural uses cover precise planting, harvesting and sorting, offering continuous operation to lessen seasonal labour. Retail and service applications involve shelf stocking, object retrieval and customer engagement. Military, security and inspection roles employ sensor‑equipped cobots for luggage scanning, hazardous substance detection, bomb disposal, facility inspection, cleaning and delicate manipulation, including surface inspection of the Space Rider orbiter, bomb defusing and border‑inspection assistance.

source_label: Section: 5 Rise of Cobots in Industry
response: Recent advances in robotic force‑modulation (RFM) technologies are largely shown together with collaborative robots (cobots), but these demonstrations are often limited to laboratory, table‑top, or kitchen environments. To underscore the wider industrial relevance of this pattern, the authors argue that it is necessary first to examine how industrial robotics has evolved and how it is shifting toward more collaborative robotic systems.

The authors surveyed 55 relevant articles, finding that 11 (20 %) target RFMs—almost all focusing on vision‑language agents (VLAs) and none on industrial applications—while only two surveys (3.6 %) explicitly address industrial contexts, both limited to narrow VLM subsets and lacking discussion of RFMs in such settings; consequently, the literature contains no dedicated review of industrial‑relevant RFMs or of broader RFM sub‑categories such as vision‑action or control‑oriented models. This gap motivates the present work, which departs from the VLA‑centric emphasis of prior surveys by providing a taxonomy‑driven overview of the full RFM landscape and a detailed analysis of the attributes and capabilities required for industrial use cases, thereby outlining how these requirements should inform future RFM design and maturity assessment.

source_label: Section: 5.3 Drivers of the Industrial Shift Toward Cobots
response: The authors describe a shift in industry from reliance on manual labour and traditional industrial robots toward greater adoption of collaborative robots (cobots). They attribute this shift to technological, organisational and economic factors that create demand for adaptable, user‑friendly, interactive automation, especially for SMEs with low‑volume, high‑mix production. Cobots are presented as having flexible design, compact footprint and easy programming that enable redeployment across tasks and locations, with user‑friendly interfaces and intuitive teach modes that reduce the need for specialised engineering expertise and integration time. They are intended to assist humans by taking over repetitive, physically demanding or hazardous work, enhancing safety and allowing workers to focus on higher‑cognitive tasks. Direct human‑robot collaboration is enabled by safety features such as real‑time sensors, force/torque monitoring and intelligent behaviour adaptation, reducing reliance on cages or barriers. Research and practice show rising cobot demand: a survey reported a >5‑fold increase in cobot‑focused publications within a decade, and global installations grew from 11 000 units in 2017 to 55 000 in 2022, with the International Federation of Robotics noting a consistent rise in the cobot‑to‑traditional‑robot proportion. Advances in computer vision and adaptive control extend cobot capabilities, aligning with Industry 4.0 goals of flexible, autonomous, and connected smart factories.

The authors note that cobots, while useful for routine and ergonomic tasks, still cannot autonomously manage complex, cognitive, or dexterous processes and lack real‑time hazard detection, continuous safe operation, and trustworthy HRI/HRC, making trust and transparency critical success factors. They argue that RFMs, integrated into cobot platforms, could address these challenges by enabling intuitive instruction, autonomous decision‑making, and real‑time adaptation via natural language, multisensor fusion, and advanced reasoning. Consequently, they call for research that moves RFMs beyond controlled labs into robust, safety‑critical industrial settings, emphasizing RFMs’ high potential to shape next‑generation collaborative robotics while also exposing current RFM limitations.

source_label: Section: 5 Rise of Cobots in Industry
response: The authors note that recent advances in robotic force‑modulation (RFM) technologies are predominantly shown in conjunction with collaborative robots (cobots), but that these demonstrations are frequently limited to laboratory, table‑top, or kitchen environments. They argue that, to appreciate the broader industrial relevance of this trend, it is necessary first to review the historical development of industrial robotics and the shift toward more collaborative robotic systems. This contextual framing is presented as a prerequisite for understanding how RFM progress, currently shown in constrained settings, might translate to wider industrial applications.

The authors state that assessing RFMs for industry requires understanding cobot capabilities and typical deployment platforms. They note contemporary cobots lack autonomous handling of complex or cognitive tasks, a gap RFMs can fill, and that analyses must consider reach, payload, accuracy, perception, manipulation hardware, power consumption, and inference hardware. The section surveys quantitative cobot capabilities and power profiles (6.1), industrial edge computing characteristics for real‑time control and inference (6.3), and essential sensing and manipulation hardware (6.2), using survey data and representative hardware comparisons to outline technical prerequisites for integrating RFMs in cobotic settings.

The authors note that industrial deployment settings differ from laboratory environments, combining heterogeneous hardware, strict safety and compliance obligations, high reliability targets, and continuous operational pressure. To address these constraints, Section 7 first synthesises the industrial implication corpus into eleven general, domain‑agnostic requirements observed across robotics applications and supported by cobot‑ and hardware‑related considerations. It then translates these implications into a structured attribute set for fine‑grained discussion of how constraints manifest within RFMs and their ecosystem. Finally, the section consolidates the attributes into a comprehensive criteria catalogue to enable consistent, transparent evaluation of industrial maturity for current and future RFMs.

Sensors are essential for cobot operation, providing environmental perception and self‑monitoring across HRC, HRI, autonomous navigation, manipulation and real‑time task execution. Common sensor types include visual (RGB, depth, CCD, 2D/3D vision), range (LiDAR, RADAR, sonar, ultrasonic, TOF/PMD, laser scanners), dynamics (IMUs, gyroscopes, accelerometers, force/torque, tactile, pressure), position/identification (encoders, RFID, infrared, GPS, odometry, magnetic) and specialised (acoustic, thermal). Advanced applications such as RFMs benefit from sensor fusion—e.g., vision combined with proximity, inertial or force/torque—to improve robustness and accuracy, using redundant or complementary sensing for safety, compliance and reliable manipulation (e.g., visual‑tactile feedback for precise handling, force sensors to detect unwanted contact). End‑effectors—grippers, suction cups, dual‑stage tools, custom drills or polishers—are tailored to tasks and often embed dedicated sensors (force feedback, vision modules). Their modularity enables rapid adaptation, higher reuse and uptime, assuming comparable flexibility in control‑algorithm action space. The selection and integration of sensors and end‑effectors thus critically affect industrial cobot applicability, creating many observation‑action permutations and underscoring the need for multimodality and output flexibility in modern control algorithms.

The authors surveyed articulated anthropomorphic cobots reported by Taesi et al. [50] to quantify capabilities relevant to RFM integration. From 180 models (Table 4) the mean degree of freedom is 6.09, with most cobots having six axes. Payload statistics show a median of 5.5 kg and a mean of 8.56 kg, indicating typical designs target moderate loads; extreme outliers reach 170 kg. Reach has a median of 910 mm (mean 970 mm) and accuracy a median of 0.05 mm (mean 0.09 mm). Table 5 summarizes 63 cobots with payloads 0.5–20 kg: mean TCP velocity 1.68 m s⁻¹ (median 1.1 m s⁻¹) and mean power consumption 0.31 kW (median 0.25 kW), with minima of 0.2 m s⁻¹ and 0.06 kW and maxima of 6 m s⁻¹ and 0.9 kW. The authors contrast these values with conventional industrial robots, whose average power is ≈3 kW and peaks up to 12–15 kW, highlighting cobots’ lower energy demand. They note that modest power requirements benefit operational cost, enable use in limited‑power settings, and support mobile or battery‑powered deployments, making efficient, low‑latency models essential for real‑time control within constrained cobotic energy budgets.

The authors describe edge PCs as the preferred platform for low‑latency cobotic AI control because they process data locally, avoiding cloud‑related latency, bandwidth and service‑interruption risks. They note that fog and cloud computing can supply scalable resources but require additional infrastructure, networking stability and incur higher latency, lower throughput and greater interruption risk for time‑critical control. Citing Ismail et al., they argue that moving computation to the edge is increasingly important for industrial deployments due to falling compute costs and reduced networking expenses.

To illustrate hardware options, the authors focus on NVIDIA Jetson devices, selecting them because the product line (Nano to Thor) is widely adopted in robotics, offers a standardized, scalable portfolio, and provides consistently documented performance, price and specification data that enable reproducible comparisons. They acknowledge that other manufacturers (Siemens, AMD/Xilinx, Intel, Advantech, Beckhoff) also supply edge devices, but comparable up‑to‑date public data for many of those alternatives are limited or unavailable.

Table 6 presents price, INT8 TOPS, memory, power draw and derived efficiency metrics for each Jetson model, together with a desktop‑class RTX 5090 GPU for reference. The RTX 5090 is not an edge device but serves as an upper‑bound benchmark; its inclusion highlights the trade‑off between workstation‑grade throughput and edge‑class energy efficiency.

From the table the authors report several trends. The Orin Nano series offers the lowest entry cost while delivering high performance per dollar, making it suitable for cost‑sensitive or large‑scale deployments. The entry‑level Xavier NX, although more expensive, provides the lowest overall AI compute performance; its 8 GB variant has the lowest maximum power consumption of all models, favoring applications where minimal energy draw is critical. Mid‑tier devices such as the Orin AGX 32 GB balance higher computational capability with moderate power requirements and emerge as the most efficient in terms of compute power per operational cost. High‑end devices (Jetson Thor series, RTX 5090) achieve substantially higher throughput but incur markedly higher energy consumption and annual operational costs, limiting their scalability for mobile, battery‑powered or energy‑constrained robots. The RTX 5090 can consume more than twice the power of a median cobot, underscoring that desktop GPUs target short, intensive workloads in energy‑abundant settings, whereas edge devices are optimized for continuous, energy‑efficient operation.

The authors also note that industrial‑class (IND) variants often include ECC memory for reliability, which can increase both initial and operational expenses and may reduce computational power relative to standard research hardware. Overall, the section concludes that deploying larger, more capable robotic foundation models must consider both compute capability and energy‑efficiency constraints to align model design with industrial practicality and operational cost.

The authors translate eleven industry‑level implications for robot‑foundation models (RFMs) into a structured set of deployment‑relevant attributes. Motivated by the need to locate expectations such as safe collaboration, robustness under uncertainty, and real‑time feasibility within an RFM system, they analyse each implication through 47 consolidated attributes that span hardware, sensing, actions, adaptation, governance and other layers (Table 7). An iterative mapping revisits every implication‑attribute pair, producing 517 cells that capture the specific industrial concerns, constraints and failure modes for each combination. This matrix‑based view highlights inter‑dependencies (e.g., safety with perception, real‑time feasibility with interaction) and aims to avoid under‑representing requirements that might otherwise be subsumed under a single headline. The resulting attribute set serves as a compact intermediate representation that makes explicit which viewpoints informed the criteria catalogue (Section 7.3) and provides traceable coverage of the industrial concerns extracted from the implication corpus (Section 7.1). The full matrix is not reproduced due to size, but the attribute list underpins a subsequent assessment framework for evaluating existing RFMs against industrial readiness.

The authors surveyed 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs, evaluating each against 149 implication‑grounded criteria (Section 7.3) to produce per‑paper maturity scores and implication‑wise profiles. They detail the evaluation methodology and scaling design for the 48,276 criterion decisions (Section 8.1), and report an agreement/consistency check with 28 expert judgments on a small ground‑truth subset. Sections 8.2 and 8.3 present the top‑performing models and an industrial applicability analysis for the full corpus and the Top‑50 subset, which together characterize current industrial maturity, highlight well‑ and poorly‑addressed implications, and form a baseline for the synthesis and outlook in Section 9.

Industrial edge PCs are positioned close to cobots to meet low‑latency, real‑time AI control needs, avoiding cloud‑related delays and networking costs; the authors focus on NVIDIA Jetson devices because their performance, pricing and specifications are publicly documented, while noting that other manufacturers (Siemens, AMD/Xilinx, Intel, Advantech, Beckhoff) lack comparable up‑to‑date data. Table 6 shows that the Orin Nano series offers the lowest purchase price with high TOPS‑per‑dollar efficiency, the Orin AGX 32 GB provides the best compute‑per‑operational‑cost balance, and the high‑end Thor series and RTX 5090 deliver maximal throughput but incur substantially higher power draw and annual costs, making them unsuitable for mobile or energy‑constrained robots. The authors also remark that industrial‑class (IND) devices often include ECC memory for reliability, which can increase both initial and operational expenses or reduce computational power relative to standard research hardware.

source_label: Section: 7.3 Evaluating Industrial Maturity: A Criteria Catalogue
response:
The authors note that the eleven industrial implications identified in Section 7.1 describe recurring demands on deployed robotic systems, but that for robot‑foundation models (RFMs) these demands must be expressed concretely in terms of model capabilities, interfaces, and the surrounding deployment stack. Building on the 517 implication‑attribute combinations from Section 7.2, they translate the implication‑grounded requirements into an explicit criteria catalogue intended to reason about, compare, and rate the industrial readiness of existing and future RFMs.  

For each implication‑attribute pair they collect and refine key deployment questions (e.g., behavior under distribution shifts, failure detection and handling, interpretation and verification of human input, required artefacts for audit and integration). Iterative consolidation yields a catalogue of 149 criteria (Table C4, Appendix) that span all eleven general industrial implications. The catalogue is presented as a living foundation that can be extended as new industrial constraints or regulatory expectations emerge.  

The scope of the criteria covers both RFMs and their deployment ecosystem. While most criteria target the model directly, the authors emphasize that industrial readiness also depends on the robot software stack, interfaces, safety infrastructure, monitoring, logging, and documentation. Accordingly, criteria are classified as (a) primarily RFM‑centric (e.g., adaptive behavior under changing observations/actions), (b) primarily ecosystem‑centric (e.g., accessible documentation on training‑data composition and transfer behavior), or (c) requiring joint model‑ecosystem support (e.g., structured signals that can be persistently logged and leveraged).  

Because the industrial implications are inter‑dependent, certain criteria deliberately re‑appear across different implications with different emphases. The authors avoid merging superficially similar criteria so that each instance preserves the aspect essential for assessing maturity with respect to a particular implication (e.g., hot‑swapping appears under adaptability, integration/cost, and perception, each stressing a distinct industrial concern).  

The catalogue reflects several key paradigms that are rarely discussed jointly in prior work and are often not yet implemented in current RFMs, though many are being investigated as separate research directions. Central motifs include:  

* **Multi‑hardware support, hot‑swapping, and dimensionality adaptation** – recent work on unified action representations and architectures handling differing action/observation spaces aligns with the catalogue’s emphasis on transfer across morphologies and runtime resilience to interface changes.  
* **Out‑of‑distribution (OOD) robustness** – industrial environments feature disturbances, clutter, and unseen conditions, motivating repeated criteria on online detection, confidence signaling, and fallback behavior. Emerging evidence of security weaknesses inherited from LLMs/VLMs (textual and vision‑side attacks) underscores that adversarial robustness cannot be optional. Anomaly prediction via forecasting action outcomes further supports the catalogue’s requirements for threat/attack detection, anomaly handling, and explicit recovery pathways.  
* **Uncertainty quantification and confidence calibration** – multiple criteria address operational readiness, safety margins, real‑time compliance, perceptual certainty, and velocity/precision‑accuracy fulfillment, reflecting the view that trust requires calibrated estimates. Recent work on confidence calibration for VLAs and statistically guaranteed help‑seeking behavior in LLM‑based planning provides supporting evidence.  
* **Interactive clarification and feedback** – criteria on human‑robot interaction/collaboration emphasize handling ambiguous or incomplete natural‑language instructions, generating follow‑up questions, and enabling mid‑execution trajectory adjustments via operator‑in‑the‑loop refinement. Studies show that interactive supervision can improve immediate reliability and collect data for future refinement.  
* **Supervisory or verification layers** – decoupled safety gating, redundant safety mechanisms, fault categorization, and explainable recovery are supported by work on VLM‑based reactive/proactive failure detection, task‑agnostic failure detectors, and bridging high‑level failure understanding to low‑level corrective actions.  
* **Memory, data governance, and documentation** – lightweight memory modules improve long‑horizon performance; frameworks that summarize prior experience aid failure reasoning and replanning; privacy‑preserving training mechanisms highlight data‑protection constraints; dataset construction that deliberately includes failures underscores the need for training data covering edge cases. These developments justify criteria on persistent logging, memory mechanisms, data‑composition variation, transparency, privacy compliance, and learning from faults.  

The authors conclude that many catalogue requirements correspond to active research directions; the industrial immaturity lies less in the absence of isolated technical proposals than in the lack of their systematic combination into a deployable, auditable, safety‑governed RFM ecosystem. The criteria catalogue therefore consolidates these partially disconnected strands into a unified, implication‑grounded assessment framework tailored to industrial operational constraints. It translates implication‑level requirements into concrete items that can be used to analyze where current RFMs are industrially mature, where they are incomplete, and which research directions are needed for credible industrial uptake. The subsequent survey section uses this framework to evaluate existing RFMs and highlight gaps between current capabilities and implication‑derived expectations.

The authors synthesized a domain‑agnostic set of industrial implications from 125 manually reviewed works by extracting statements about recurring requirements, constraints, and deployment challenges, clustering them, and iteratively refining the clusters into eleven compact implications. They observed no outright contradictions; instead, themes overlapped, with the same practical challenge (e.g., human presence) appearing under different lenses such as safety, interaction design, robustness, or perception, and they preserved these overlaps by separating what is demanded from why it is demanded.

Implication 1 (Adaptability & Flexibility) is motivated by repeated observations that real deployments are highly variable: processes change, product variants proliferate, and boundary conditions shift, increasing re‑parameterisation effort and uncertainty. Traditional automation is described as brittle under minor changes, whereas industry expects robots and control methods that can adjust behaviour online, be reconfigurable across products and processes, and reduce costly reprogramming cycles, especially in dynamic, partially known, or unstructured environments and when humans are present. Sector‑specific discussions note that lighting, weather, and clutter also affect operation, requiring robust handling.

Implication 2 (Safety & Compliance) is framed as a gating factor for deployment, particularly in shared workspaces and high‑consequence settings. Safety‑aware control logic is required for cobots, which must prevent injuries, be tested, certified, and equipped with appropriate safety features. The literature links safety to standards and certification frameworks (e.g., ISO 10218, ISO/TS 15066) and stresses that safety must be maintained under dynamic, unpredictable conditions, including human behavioural variability and sensing uncertainty. Overly conservative safety mechanisms can reduce efficiency, motivating integrated safety‑aware reasoning that preserves productivity.

Implication 3 (Human‑Robot Interaction & Collaboration) reflects a vision of industrial robotics as human‑centric, with robots and humans working in proximity or physical collaboration to combine human flexibility and cognition with robotic repeatability and precision. The literature distinguishes multiple interaction regimes (coexistence, cooperation, collaboration; remote, proximity, physical) and calls for diverse interface and coordination solutions. Direct physical collaboration requires perception of contact and appropriate response. Communication quality, interface usability, and intuitive, natural modalities (e.g., speech) are repeatedly emphasized to reduce reliance on expert programming and support real‑time operator involvement. Reactive methods that handle uncertainty are needed to maintain fluid workflows.

Implication 4 (Robustness & Reliability) is motivated by characterisations of industrial environments as uncertain, noisy, and disturbance‑prone, with internal uncertainties (unmodelled dynamics, friction, delays) and external uncertainties (measurement errors, environmental noise). The literature calls for robust methodologies that integrate perception, planning, and control under uncertainty, and for reliability mechanisms such as monitoring and timely status updates to support reactive planning. Robustness is extended to include resilience against faulty sensors, out‑of‑distribution inputs, and adversarial or cybersecurity threats, with expectations for stable operation, fault awareness, and meaningful status reporting.

Implication 5 (Precision & Accuracy) is highlighted despite the emphasis on flexibility. Industrial competitiveness is linked to efficiency and accuracy; tasks require high precision, repeatability, and quality‑critical execution. Accuracy concerns both actuation and sensing, with noted gaps in grasping and positioning accuracy in demanding settings. Vision‑/language‑guided control is identified as lacking the precision required for industrial use, motivating improved sensing and motion‑planning accuracy while retaining flexibility.

Implication 6 (Real‑Time Performance) is presented as a pervasive constraint across sensing, decision‑making, interaction, and control. The literature references action‑level and task‑level timing requirements, real‑time communication, and motion control. Real‑time sensing and processing are needed for dynamic scenes, multi‑modal integration, and sudden responses, yet data‑driven methods often face computational complexity and large training/inference demands, especially on edge devices with limited power. Real‑time planning in dynamic scenes remains an unresolved challenge, though smaller models may enable real‑time inference.

Implication 7 (Cost‑Effectiveness & Integration Capabilities) is framed by the need for economic justification, especially for low‑volume production and SMEs. High system cost is cited as a barrier; frequent product changes increase reprogramming effort and cost, motivating approaches that reduce commissioning overhead and ease reconfiguration. Integration is described as a practical obstacle due to lacking community‑wide standards and guidelines, with specific concerns about integrating state‑of‑the‑art components into factory architectures. Scalability, cost‑sensitive hardware, and efficient deployment on low‑power edge devices are emphasized.

Implication 8 (Explainability & Trust) links AI‑driven robotics adoption to transparency, interpretability, and operator trust, especially where failures have severe consequences. Explainability mechanisms and user interfaces for presenting explanations are seen as key enablers. Limited adoption of perception models is attributed to difficulty in understanding and trusting outputs under failure risk. Trust is discussed as a determinant of acceptance in collaborative work, with psychological and ergonomic aspects (comfort, safety perception) and the need for visibility into system status and feedback. Limitations in sensing and flexibility can negatively affect perceived safety and trust.

Implication 9 (Sensor Fusion & Perception) is motivated by the view that perception is a central capability limiting automation scope, particularly in shared and variable environments. No single modality suffices; multi‑modal sensing and fusion are required to handle occlusions, dust, lighting variation, and sensor degradation. Fusion of vision, tactile, and other sensors supports safe collaboration and robust perception pipelines. Control systems must accommodate heterogeneous and evolving observation spaces, reflecting the diverse sensor configurations common with cobots.

Section: 7.3 Evaluating Industrial Maturity: A Criteria Catalogue
response: The authors derived a catalogue of 149 industrial‑readiness criteria for robotic foundation models (RFMs) by mapping 517 implication‑attribute combinations from Section 7.1 into concrete questions about distribution‑shift handling, failure detection, human‑input verification, and audit artefacts, explicitly covering model‑centric, ecosystem‑centric, and joint requirements and retaining intentional redundancy to diagnose immaturity in specific dimensions. They illustrate that most criteria align with emerging research on multi‑hardware support, hot‑swapping, OOD robustness, confidence calibration, interactive clarification, supervisory safety layers, memory, data governance and documentation, citing recent VLA/LLM works that address these motifs. Consequently, the catalogue serves as a living, implication‑grounded framework to assess current RFMs, identify gaps, and guide systematic integration of disparate technical advances toward auditable, safety‑governed industrial deployment.

The authors evaluated industrial readiness for all 324 manipulation‑capable or generalist robot‑foundation models (RFMs) in their models sub‑corpus (out of 341 total publications) by applying an automated, large‑scale LLM‑based pipeline. Each paper was checked against 149 implication‑grounded criteria, producing 48 276 criterion‑level decisions. Manual annotation was deemed infeasible, so the pipeline used GPT‑5.1 to extract evidence from each paper and decide, for each criterion, whether it was fulfilled. To prevent cross‑contamination, every evaluation run isolated a single criterion and a single paper in a dedicated vector store that was deleted after the decision; sessions were closed before the next pair. All processing occurred on private Siemens infrastructure, avoiding public upload and training use, thereby mitigating disclosure or copyright risks.

For each paper‑criterion pair the LLM output a binary fulfilment judgment, a flag for direct statement, a confidence score (0–1), an evidence‑availability flag, extracted quotes (or a statement of no relevant information), and a brief rationale. The LLM was instructed to be conservative: unclear or out‑of‑scope criteria were marked unfulfilled, yielding intentionally cautious maturity estimates, especially for partially addressed capabilities.

Reliability was assessed on a small expert‑rated subset of three papers (two annotated before, one after the pipeline run). Table 8 shows that the LLM reproduced expert implication‑level patterns, confirming that Gemini Robotics 1.5 scores higher than OpenVLA, while π0 remains limited. Criterion‑level agreement across 447 decisions was high (accuracy 0.966, F1 0.762 for the positive class, Cohen’s κ 0.744). The false‑positive rate was low (1.9 %), but the false‑negative rate was higher (22.6 %) consistent with the conservative policy, so maturity values should be viewed as lower‑bound estimates. Filtering by the “information‑found” flag did not improve F1 and slightly reduced κ, indicating it mainly reflects evidence presence rather than correctness.

Per‑paper agreement was strong for Gemini Robotics 1.5 and OpenVLA (high κ and Jaccard similarity), but lower for π0, where the expert positive rate was only 2.7 % and metrics dropped accordingly; the authors note that few positives can inflate disagreement metrics. Some disagreements stem from interpretive differences: e.g., experts considered a modest increase in task success rate as sufficient for “Mid‑Execution Feedback Responsiveness,” whereas the LLM required explicit course‑correction capability. Other cases involved criteria with ambiguous thresholds, such as “Low‑Data Adaptation & Few‑Shot Requirements,” where OpenVLA’s reported 10‑150 episodes led the LLM to mark the criterion fulfilled, while experts deemed up to 150 episodes too demanding for industrial readiness. Conversely, stringent criteria demanding guarantees like “always” caused the LLM to mark them unfulfilled even when implementations existed without absolute guarantees.

Overall, the comparison indicates that the pipeline yields reliable, conservative maturity estimates suitable for scaling assessments across hundreds of RFMs. The low over‑claiming rate supports its use for model comparison and identifying implication‑level gaps, while the higher miss rate and interpretive latitude of some criteria advise caution when interpreting individual criterion outcomes. Consequently, the authors focus subsequent analysis on implication‑level trends rather than fine‑grained criterion results.

The authors synthesized 125 manually reviewed industrial works into eleven inter‑dependent implications that capture dominant industrial expectations for robotic systems and, by extension, for learning‑based control and foundation‑model approaches: (1) adaptability and flexibility to handle frequent task, process and environment variation without costly reprogramming; (2) safety and compliance with standards (e.g., ISO 10218, ISO/TS 15066) and robust operation under uncertainty, failures and OOD inputs; (3) human‑robot interaction and collaboration requiring natural, intuitive communication, continuous operator involvement and reactive methods for variable, partially automatable tasks; (4) robustness and reliability to maintain stable operation amid internal and external uncertainties, sensor degradation, adversarial and cybersecurity threats, with fault awareness; (5) precision and accuracy in actuation and perception to meet quality‑critical, high‑throughput demands; (6) real‑time performance across sensing, decision‑making and control despite limited compute budgets and edge‑device constraints; (7) cost‑effectiveness and integration capabilities that reduce manual effort, commissioning overhead and enable scalable deployment on heterogeneous, resource‑limited hardware; (8) explainability and trust through transparent, interpretable outputs and ergonomic interfaces that support acceptance and safe collaboration; (9) sensor fusion and perception pipelines that combine multimodal data to overcome single‑sensor limitations and support safe, reliable operation; and (10) standardized benchmarking and evaluation to provide reproducible, task‑relevant assessments, while (11) data requirements and usage acknowledge data scarcity, costly collection, sim‑to‑real gaps and the need for data‑efficient, continual‑learning methods. These implications are presented as adoption bottlenecks that explain why many laboratory‑grade learning approaches struggle to translate into production environments and form the basis for subsequent industrial readiness assessments.

The authors examined industrial applicability of robot‑function‑modelling (RFM) research by analysing all 324 evaluated papers (the “full corpus”) and a subset of the 50 highest‑ranked models (the “Top‑50”). Their analysis used two quantitative metrics per implication: (1) 1+‑Coverage, the proportion of papers meeting at least one criterion for a given implication (breadth), and (2) Average Criteria Coverage (ACC), the average fraction of criteria met per paper for that implication (depth). They also inspected temporal trends, the most frequently fulfilled criteria, and a “gap” analysis comparing evidence availability with fulfilment rates.

**Temporal stability** – Normalised per‑implication criterion‑fulfilment ratios (Figure 11) show a stable pattern across publication years 2020‑2025. A small set of implications consistently dominates: adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking/evaluation (I10), and data requirements/usage (I11). In contrast, safety/compliance (I2), human‑robot interaction/collaboration (I3), real‑time performance (I6), and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7) remain persistently low. No monotonic increase in any implication’s coverage is observed, indicating that RFM research has not yet moved toward more holistic industrial coverage.

**Breadth versus depth** – Figure 12 and Table 13 reveal a systematic breadth‑depth mismatch. In the full corpus, only I1 (0.756), I10 (0.753) and I11 (0.707) achieve high 1+‑Coverage; all other implications have 1+‑Coverage below 0.22. However, ACC values for these leading implications stay below 0.10 (I10 0.099, I11 0.097, I1 0.089), meaning papers typically satisfy only a small fraction of the criteria within the implications they address. Safety/compliance (I2 0.034), HRI/HRC (I3 0.052), real‑time performance (I6 0.049) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7 0.071) are especially weak even at the breadth level.

In the Top‑50 subset, breadth becomes near‑universal for seven implications (I1, I4, I5, I8, I9, I10, I11 all reach 1.0 1+‑Coverage). Nevertheless, depth remains limited: the highest ACC values are again concentrated in I1 (0.238), I10 (0.232) and I11 (0.227). Safety/compliance (I2 0.019) and real‑time performance (I6 0.036) stay particularly low, and even the strongest papers show only modest multi‑criterion coverage.

**Most frequently fulfilled criteria** – Table 14 lists the ten criteria with the highest fulfilment rates across all papers. They cluster in the three dominant implications: Multi‑Task Generalisation (I1, 0.4938), Flexible Data Type Acceptance (I11, 0.4877), Repeatability & Reproducibility (I10, 0.4475), Low‑Data Adaptation & Few‑Shot Requirements (I11, 0.4198), and several benchmarking‑related criteria (I10). Explicitness of fulfilment is low for some of these (e.g., Multi‑Task Generalisation 0.2812, Repeatability 0.2483), suggesting that fulfilment is often inferred from experiments rather than directly stated. Low‑Data Adaptation shows higher explicitness (0.8088), reflecting its frequent explicit claim as a contribution, though the authors note that interpretation latitude may inflate its rate.

**Evidence‑fulfilled gap** – Table 15 reports, for each implication, the criterion with the highest evidence rate, its evidence‑rate (EvidRate), fulfilment rate (FulfillRate), and the resulting gap score (gc = EvidRate − FulfillRate). Gap scores are large for almost every implication, frequently exceeding 0.8, indicating that many criteria are widely discussed or documentable but rarely satisfied under the binary fulfilment policy. For example, I2’s top criterion (Reactive, Real‑Time Safety) has EvidRate 0.8117 but FulfillRate 0.0031 (gc 0.8086); I3’s Collaborative Adaptation shows EvidRate 0.8981 vs. FulfillRate 0.0247 (gc 0.8735). Similar large gaps appear for I6, I7 and I8. The authors interpret these gaps, together with low ACC values, as evidence that the literature increasingly acknowledges industrial constraints but still delivers only limited, criterion‑incomplete solutions, especially for implications tied to deployment integration (I7), safety/compliance (I2), real‑time performance (I6) and HRC/HRI (I3).

**Conclusions** – The industrial applicability analysis shows that RFM research consistently focuses on a narrow set of implications (adaptability, benchmarking, data usage) while neglecting others critical for deployment. Even the top‑performing papers broaden their coverage but do not substantially increase depth. The most commonly fulfilled criteria align with expectations of adaptable, data‑flexible systems, yet explicit reporting of these criteria is often low. Large evidence‑fulfilment gaps across most implications suggest that, despite growing discussion of industrial requirements, actual implementations remain partial. The authors therefore conclude that current RFM literature is not yet converging toward comprehensive, holistically industrially mature solutions.

Industrial robotics is shifting from isolated, highly optimised automation toward flexible, collaborative deployment where humans and robots share workspaces. This transition is driven by cobot uptake in high‑mix, low‑volume settings and SMEs, where traditional automation is often impractical because of commissioning effort, frequent production changes, and the need for specialised expertise. Modern cobots provide safe physical design, appropriate payload and sizing, and low operating power, but they do not solve the central bottleneck: robust, deployment‑ready intelligence that can adapt behaviour to changing tasks, environments and multimodal input without prohibitive engineering overhead.

The authors frame robot foundation models (RFMs) as a promising enabling technology because they target multi‑task competence, cross‑domain generalisation, and instruction‑ or demonstration‑driven low‑effort reconfiguration—dimensions where classical control and specialised learning‑based approaches remain limited. However, the same factors that make cobot deployments attractive—shared workspaces, continuous operation, heterogeneous actuation/sensing stacks and cost pressure—amplify demands on learning‑based control. Typical cobots exhibit high mechanical precision, moderate payload, and low median power draw (0.5‑20 kg class), implying that industrial value is often limited by perception and decision‑making under real‑world variability rather than actuation quality, and that RFM deployment must operate with low‑latency, energy‑aware inference on edge platforms rather than workstation‑grade hardware. Multi‑sensor configurations, sensor fusion and modular end‑effectors further require interface‑flexible intelligence that tolerates changing observation and action spaces.

To capture these realities, the authors distilled eleven interdependent industrial implications, extracted 47 deployment‑relevant attributes, and built an implication‑attribute matrix (11 × 47 = 517 considerations) that yielded a criteria catalogue of 149 concrete items spanning model capabilities and ecosystem requirements. Their assessment of 324 discovered RFMs (48,276 criterion‑level decisions) shows that even top‑ranked models achieve only 0.11‑0.12 overall maturity—roughly one‑tenth of criteria met on average—and most models score highly on at most two to three implications. The strongest systems exhibit implication‑wise “peaks” (e.g., structured reasoning, human‑in‑the‑loop interaction, self‑correction) rather than balanced coverage; Gemini Robotics 1.5 leads overall and scores highest on adaptability/flexibility (I1 = 0.44) but is near zero on several deployment‑critical implications. Models that perform well in HRI/HRC or perception emphasise collaborative mechanisms and richer observation handling but do not satisfy the broader criteria needed for sustained industrial operation. Across the full corpus, research consistently concentrates on adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking/evaluation (I10) and data requirements/usage (I11), while safety/compliance (I2), HRI/HRC (I3), real‑time performance (I6) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7) remain persistently underrepresented. Breadth‑depth analysis confirms that many papers touch several implications but few satisfy a substantial fraction of criteria within them; even the Top‑50 subset shows modest depth for leading implications and weak coverage for deployment‑critical ones.

The authors propose concrete priorities: move from isolated capability demonstrations to deployable, layered systems where planning, memory, action generation, verification and safety gating are central, independently testable components; develop evaluation protocols and artefacts that connect RFM capabilities to operational constraints such as low‑latency edge inference, structured logging, monitoring and handling of changing sensor/tooling interfaces; leverage the strong emphasis on benchmarking to create evaluations that reflect deployment realities (distribution shifts, failure recovery, human supervision, long‑horizon operation) and diagnose failure causes; and close large evidence‑fulfilment gaps, especially in safety/compliance, HRI/HRC, real‑time performance and cost‑effectiveness/integration. In conclusion, RFMs constitute a credible pathway to unlock cobot‑centred automation by targeting flexibility, reconfigurability and intuitive instruction, yet current RFM research remains predominantly laboratory‑oriented relative to deployment‑grounded industrial requirements. The presented implication synthesis and criteria catalogue provide a transparent industrial‑readiness reference to evaluate and guide future RFMs toward auditable, safe, real‑time‑capable and integration‑ready systems.

response: The analysis of 324 RFMs (and the Top‑50 subset) shows a stable focus over 2020‑2025 on adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking/evaluation (I10) and data requirements/usage (I11), while safety/compliance (I2), HRI/HRC (I3), real‑time performance (I6) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7) remain consistently under‑addressed; breadth (1+‑Coverage) is high only for I1 (0.756), I10 (0.753) and I11 (0.707) but depth (ACC) stays below 0.10 for all, even in the Top‑50 where ACC improves modestly (e.g., I1 0.238, I10 0.232, I11 0.227). The ten most frequently fulfilled criteria cluster in I1, I10 and I11, yet explicitness is low for many (e.g., Multi‑Task Generalisation 0.2812), and gap analysis reveals large evidence‑fulfilment gaps (gc often > 0.8), indicating that criteria are widely discussed but rarely satisfied, especially for deployment‑related implications (I2, I3, I6, I7).

Industrial robotics is shifting toward collaborative cobot deployment, but robust, adaptable intelligence remains the bottleneck; RFMs promise multi‑task competence, cross‑domain generalisation, and low‑effort reconfiguration, yet must meet low‑latency, energy‑aware edge constraints and tolerate changing sensor‑actuator configurations. Our assessment of 324 models using 149 criteria shows the field is rapidly expanding in breadth but early in industrial maturity, with top models meeting only ~0.11‑0.12 of criteria and excelling in isolated implications (e.g., adaptability) while lagging in safety, HRI/HRC, real‑time performance, and integration. Closing these gaps through layered architectures, edge‑ready inference, structured logging, and evaluation protocols that reflect deployment realities is identified as the central research agenda for achieving reliable, industry‑grade RFMs.

Implication Category/ Criterion
I1: A. Multi-Hardware and Configuration Adaptability
Adaptability & 1. Multi-Hardware Support: Operates with different kinematics, sensors, and
Flexibility end-effectors without retraining.
2. Hot-Swappable & Dimensionality Adaptation: Sensors/actuators can be replaced,
added, or removed during operation. Automatically detects and configures
input/output channels at runtime according to connected hardware and environmental
context: Flexibly adapts the dimensionality, type and interpretation without manual
intervention or system restart.
B. Task Adaptability and Strategy Flexibility
3. Multi-Task Generalisation: Handles multiple task types/categories, including unseen
variations thereof, without retraining. Adapts strategies dynamically for task variations
and can switch between tasks online.
4. Restricted Autonomous Task Switching: Only switches between distinct tasks upon
explicit user instruction: autonomy remains bounded, so adherence to the operator’s
goal stays primary (may autonomously adapt solution approaches/ strategies).
5. Strategy-Goal Alignment: Any adaptation of solution strategies ensures adherence to
the commanded task goal: deviating too far from user instructions triggers feedback,
halt, or request for approval.
C. Environmental Adaptation and Robustness
6. Generalisation to Environmental Variation: Maintains consistent performance across
diverse environmental conditions (lighting, weather, background, friction, etc.),
object/material variations, and scene clutter, with minimal degradation.
7. Autonomous Handling of Distractors/Obstacles: Identifies and robustly manages/
handles unknown, distracting, or non-required objects in the scene or obstacles along
the path/ trajectory (including incorporation into task strategy if needed).
8. Online Environment Adaptation & Response: Recognises and continuously adapts to
environmental changes, such as errors, faults, sensor degradation or external influences
during operation: e.g. logging, halting, or feedback-requesting as confidence drops.
9. Autonomous Fallbacks: Capable of autonomously choosing context-appropriate
error/fault responses (e.g. request feedback, switch input modalities, logging, etc.) and
behaviour (e.g. continue operation, transition to safe state, adapt strategy, etc.)
without requiring predefined fallback behaviour.
D. Instruction and Feedback Flexibility
10. Multimodal Command Interface: Accepts user-input (task instructions,
correction/feedback, etc.) via diverse modalities (natural language in multiple
languages, images, teaching by demonstration, video, etc.).
11. Mid-Execution Feedback Responsiveness: Remains receptive to user feedback and
correction throughout execution, enabling course correction and adjustment without
re-initiating trajectories.
E. Self-Flexibility and Adaptive Behaviour

Implication Category/ Criterion
12. Operational Adaptation Confidence: Continuously outputs a confidence score
reflecting its present predicted ability to execute the instructed task using the currently
(adapted) solution strategy, in the current environment, with the currently active
hardware configuration and sensor context. The score may be used to trigger automatic
logging, operator feedback requests, or safe halting if confidence drops below a set
threshold, ensuring transparent awareness and operational safety during dynamic
adaptation.
13. Autonomous Incorporation of Skills: Dynamically selects and integrates known
robot skills (e.g. action primitives) as needed for current task/environment into the
current solution strategy (like tool-calling).
14. Online/Mid-Execution Adaptation: Integrates operator/environmental feedback,
(input/ task)-quality degradation and detected faults dynamically during operation,
adapting strategy, input importance or output.
15. Explained Adaptation Decisions: Explains, upon request, its performed/ intended
adaptation of strategies, handling of distractors, input importance/quality (for each
modality), and response to uncertainties or noise.
16. Memory of Previous Faults/Distractors: Remembers prior encountered variations,
distractors, faults, anomalies, environmental changes and corresponding solutions,
reducing the need for repeated user intervention for recurring scenarios.
17. Energy/System-Aware Adaptation: Adapts solution strategies and predicted actions
based on real-time resource constraints and consumption (e.g. battery charge, system
health, energy/ compute utilisation).
18. Self-Evaluation & Command Adherence: Continuously self-evaluates its own
adapted behaviour and adherence to user command(s): Flags or readjusts if deviation
from expected outcome or operator intent is detected.
I2: A. Verification, Standards, and Certification
Safety & 1. Standards-Compliant: Behaviour and safety features are checked to align with
Compliance relevant industrial standards, evaluated by reproducible tests.
2. Integrable Safety Systems: System interfaces and safety signals are compatible with
industrial plant safety infrastructure, supporting seamless integration and monitoring
(e.g. model-generated safety stop can be directly used to stop respective production line).
3. Safety Documentation & Traceability: All safety features, integration, and reasoning
are well documented, including considered safety rules, internal processes, output
explanations, and verified compliance with standards.
B. Safety Reasoning, Adaptation, and Confidence
4. Safety Confidence Output: Outputs a confidence score estimating the safety margin
of each predicted operation and for the complete task before starting operation (in the
current environment). The confidence score quantifies the system’s estimated likelihood
that all specified safety requirements are currently satisfied, using
sensor/hardware/context data.
5. Persistence of Safety Capabilities in Adaptation: Safety rules/modules remain
enforced, and system safety is verified after any model adaptation, retraining, or
finetuning →standalone safety logic cannot be bypassed by learning changes.
6. Reactive, Real-Time Safety: System performs continuous, real-time evaluation of
safety (considering sensor noise, hardware degradation, dynamic obstacles, harmful
objects, OOD, and environment changes) – e.g. leveraging confidence – with immediate
adaptation (halting/ triggering stop, slowing, or replanning) if risks arise.

I1: A. Multi-Hardware and Configuration Adaptability
Adaptability & 1. Multi-Hardware Support: Operates with different kinematics, sensors, and
Flexibility end-effectors without retraining.
2. Hot-Swappable & Dimensionality Adaptation: Sensors/actuators can be replaced,
added, or removed during operation. Automatically detects and configures
input/output channels at runtime according to connected hardware and environmental
context: Flexibly adapts the dimensionality, type and interpretation without manual
intervention or system restart.
B. Task Adaptability and Strategy Flexibility
3. Multi-Task Generalisation: Handles multiple task types/categories, including unseen
variations thereof, without retraining. Adapts strategies dynamically for task variations
and can switch between tasks online.
4. Restricted Autonomous Task Switching: Only switches between distinct tasks upon
explicit user instruction: autonomy remains bounded, so adherence to the operator’s
goal stays primary (may autonomously adapt solution approaches/ strategies).
5. Strategy-Goal Alignment: Any adaptation of solution strategies ensures adherence to
the commanded task goal: deviating too far from user instructions triggers feedback,
halt, or request for approval.
C. Environmental Adaptation and Robustness
6. Generalisation to Environmental Variation: Maintains consistent performance across
diverse environmental conditions (lighting, weather, background, friction, etc.),
object/material variations, and scene clutter, with minimal degradation.
7. Autonomous Handling of Distractors/Obstacles: Identifies and robustly manages/
handles unknown, distracting, or non-required objects in the scene or obstacles along
the path/ trajectory (including incorporation into task strategy if needed).
8. Online Environment Adaptation & Response: Recognises and continuously adapts to
environmental changes, such as errors, faults, sensor degradation or external influences
during operation: e.g. logging, halting, or feedback-requesting as confidence drops.
9. Autonomous Fallbacks: Capable of autonomously choosing context-appropriate
error/fault responses (e.g. request feedback, switch input modalities, logging, etc.) and
behaviour (e.g. continue operation, transition to safe state, adapt strategy, etc.)
without requiring predefined fallback behaviour.
D. Instruction and Feedback Flexibility
10. Multimodal Command Interface: Accepts user-input (task instructions,
correction/feedback, etc.) via diverse modalities (natural language in multiple
languages, images, teaching by demonstration, video, etc.).
11. Mid-Execution Feedback Responsiveness: Remains receptive to user feedback and
correction throughout execution, enabling course correction and adjustment without
re-initiating trajectories.
E. Self-Flexibility and Adaptive Behaviour
